analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying for life and creates a public lobbying database.
analysis.headline: The bill has received no committee action and no cosponsors since being referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently bar former members of Congress from ever working as lobbyists, extend the lobbying ban for congressional staff from one year to six years, and ban lobbyists from joining the office of any member they recently lobbied for six years. It would also create a single public website (lobbyists.gov) where anyone could search lobbying disclosures and see which lobbying firms hire former congressional insiders, and it would raise the maximum fine for breaking lobbying disclosure rules from $200,000 to $500,000. The bill was introduced by Sen. Michael Bennet and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would gain a clearer window into who is lobbying whom: a single searchable public website of lobbying activity and of lobbying firms' former-Congress hires, plus stronger restrictions on ex-lawmakers returning as lobbyists. The public as a whole would benefit if lawmaking were less shaped by former members and staff paid to represent paying clients. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters worried about money in politics

how_it_helps.text: It would end the practice of former senators and representatives cashing in on their congressional connections by lobbying their former colleagues, with a lifetime ban backed by criminal penalties.

It would extend the 'cooling-off' period for congressional staff from one year to six years, making it harder for staffers to move straight from writing laws to lobbying for the industries they regulated or funded.
It would bar registered lobbyists and foreign agents from working for a member of Congress or committee they lobbied within the past six years, closing the door running in the other direction.

It would require lobbying firms with more than three lobbyists to publicly report every former member and senior congressional staffer they employ, listed on a single searchable public website, and send those filings to the U.S. Attorney for Washington, D.C. to check for underreporting.
It would nearly triple the maximum fine for lobbying disclosure violations, from $200,000 to $500,000, giving firms a stronger reason to file accurate reports.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and former members of Congress who make a living selling influence would bear the cost: a lifetime lobbying ban for former members, longer bans for staff, and much larger fines for lobbying disclosure violations would curtail a well-paid career path and make influence-peddling riskier. [S2]

drawbacks.text: A lifetime lobbying ban on former members of Congress is broader than any current rule and could be challenged as restricting the right of ex-lawmakers to petition the government for a living, an objection that has been raised against shorter revolving-door restrictions.
The Ethics Committees could waive the six-year lobbyist-into-Congress ban for a 'compelling national need', which creates an exception that could be used routinely in practice.

Enforcement depends on disclosure and prosecutors: the bill raises penalties and adds reporting requirements, but its main new enforcement tool is sending filings to one U.S. Attorney's office, and past lobbying disclosure rules have been enforced rarely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for ordinary people would be real but indirect: fewer former lawmakers selling influence, more visible lobbying records, and tougher penalties. The costs fall almost entirely on the lobbying industry and former members of Congress, not on taxpayers or workers. The main weaknesses are the ethics-committee waiver, which could swallow the lobbyist-into-Congress ban, and the reliance on disclosure and prosecutorial follow-through, which historically has been thin. On balance it is a well-aimed but modestly designed transparency-and-restrictions bill whose fate is being decided by inaction rather than debate.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Homeland Security committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing or vote and no cosponsors signing on.

narrative.text: The bill would impose a lifetime ban on former members of Congress lobbying Congress, extend staff lobbying bans from one year to six years, and bar lobbyists from joining offices they recently lobbied for six years.

It would create a searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, for lobbying disclosures and require large lobbying firms to report their former-congressional hires, with filings sent to the U.S. Attorney in Washington for enforcement review.
It would raise the maximum penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.

The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action — no hearing, markup, vote, or cosponsor — appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lobbying industry and former members of Congress who sell their connections are better off, because none of the proposed restrictions took effect. Lawmakers also keep the option of the revolving door for themselves and their staffs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbying industry; no limits took effect

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to impose a lifetime lobbying ban on former members, lengthen staff lobbying bans, and create a public lobbying disclosure website.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has not yet drawn votes or opposing statements; it simply has no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cut off the core business model that trades former lawmakers' access for client fees: a lifetime ban on ex-members lobbying, six-year bans on staff and on hiring recent lobbyists into congressional offices, and fines up to $500,000 for disclosure violations. A searchable public record of firms' former-Congress hires would also expose their inside connections to scrutiny.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress turned lobbyists
industries.note: Current and former members of Congress would lose the well-paid post-Congress career of lobbying for paying clients, which is a major financial incentive attached to holding office.

industries.industry: Corporate lobbying clients (major industries with Washington offices)
industries.note: Companies that rely on hiring former congressional staff to press their agendas would face a six-year cooling-off period before those insiders could work on their behalf, and would have their former-insider hires listed publicly.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and has sat untouched in the Homeland Security committee since May 2025. Ethics-restriction bills rarely advance without a champion on the committee or leadership backing, and none has appeared here. The most likely path is that it stays parked and quietly dies at the end of the 119th Congress, unless a lobbying scandal or public campaign revives interest in the bill.
